subject: biology
title: DNA replication
summary: How a cell copies its DNA: origins and forks, the enzymes at the fork, and the leading and lagging strands.

concepts.name: DNA replication
concepts.summary: Before a cell divides it copies its DNA: the two strands separate and each serves as the template for a new partner strand.

elements.name: Order of events at the fork

explain.text: Before a cell divides it makes a full copy of its DNA, so each new cell gets one. The double helix is unzipped and each old strand is used as a template: free nucleotides pair with its bases, A with T and G with C, and are joined into a new strand. The result is two double helices, each with one old strand and one new one. This is called semiconservative replication. The work happens at a Y-shaped replication fork, where a team of enzymes unwinds, primes, copies and seals the DNA.

concepts.name: Meselson-Stahl experiment
concepts.summary: The 1958 experiment that used heavy and light nitrogen to show DNA replication is semiconservative rather than conservative or dispersive.

explain.text: In 1958 Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl grew bacteria on heavy nitrogen-15 until all their DNA was heavy, then moved them to normal nitrogen-14. After each generation they spun the DNA in a density gradient, where heavier DNA settles lower. After one generation there was a single band halfway between heavy and light, so each molecule was half old and half new. After two generations there were two bands, hybrid and light. Only semiconservative replication predicts both results, so the experiment ruled out the conservative and dispersive models.

concepts.name: Origin of replication
concepts.summary: A site where replication starts: the helix opens into a bubble and two forks move away from it in opposite directions.

elements.name: One origin in bacteria, many in eukaryotes

explain.text: Replication does not start just anywhere. It begins at origins of replication, sequences where proteins bind and pull the strands apart. The opening grows into a replication bubble with a fork at each end, and the two forks move away from the origin in opposite directions until they meet other forks. A bacterium such as E. coli has one origin on its circular DNA. A human cell has tens of thousands, because its DNA is so long that copying it from one origin would take weeks. Origins are often rich in A-T pairs, which separate easily.

concepts.name: DNA helicase
concepts.summary: The enzyme that unwinds DNA at the fork by breaking the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, helped by single-strand binding proteins and topoisomerase.

explain.text: Helicase is the enzyme that opens the double helix. It is a ring of proteins that slides along one strand at the fork, using energy from ATP to break the hydrogen bonds between base pairs and push the strands apart, like a zip being opened. Two helpers work with it. Single-strand binding proteins coat the separated strands so they do not snap back together. Topoisomerase works ahead of the fork, cutting and rejoining DNA to relieve the overwinding that the unzipping causes, the way a twisted rope tightens as you pull its strands apart.

concepts.name: DNA polymerase
concepts.summary: The enzyme that builds new DNA, adding nucleotides one at a time to the 3′ end of a strand, so every new strand grows 5′ to 3′.

explain.text: DNA polymerase is the enzyme that actually builds new DNA. It reads the template strand and, for each base, picks the nucleotide that pairs with it, then bonds that nucleotide to the 3′ end of the growing strand. The incoming nucleotide arrives with three phosphates, and splitting two off pays for the new bond. Because it can only add to a 3′ end, every new strand grows in the 5′ to 3′ direction. DNA polymerase also proofreads: if it adds a wrong base it backs up, removes it and tries again, which keeps copying errors rare.

concepts.name: RNA primer
concepts.summary: A short piece of RNA, made by primase, that gives DNA polymerase a 3′ end to start from; it is later removed and replaced with DNA.

explain.text: DNA polymerase cannot start a new strand from nothing; it can only add to a strand that already has a 3′ end. An enzyme called primase solves this by building a short stretch of RNA, about ten nucleotides long, paired to the template. This RNA primer gives DNA polymerase a 3′ end to extend. The leading strand needs a primer only at its start, but the lagging strand needs a new one for every fragment. Later the RNA is removed and replaced with DNA, so no RNA is left in the finished molecule.

concepts.name: Leading and lagging strands
concepts.summary: At each fork one new strand is built continuously toward the fork and the other in short Okazaki fragments that DNA ligase joins.

explain.text: The two template strands at a fork run in opposite directions, but DNA polymerase can only build 5′ to 3′. On one template that direction points toward the fork, so the new leading strand grows smoothly as the fork opens. On the other it points away from the fork, so the lagging strand is made backwards in short pieces called Okazaki fragments. Each fragment starts from its own RNA primer. Once the primers are replaced with DNA, DNA ligase seals the gaps between fragments, joining them into one continuous strand.

items.prompt: Why is DNA replication called semiconservative?
choices: Half of the genes are copied and half are not
Each new double helix has one old strand and one new strand
One new double helix is all old DNA and the other is all new
Each strand is a patchwork of old and new pieces of DNA
items.explanation: Each daughter molecule keeps one parent strand and gains one new one. One all-old and one all-new helix is the conservative model; a patchwork of old and new is the dispersive model. Both were ruled out by experiment.

items.prompt: In replication, what is the existing strand that a new strand is built against called?
items.explanation: Each parent strand acts as a template: its bases set which nucleotides are added, by base pairing.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: A template strand reads 3′-TACGGA-5′. Which new strand is built against it?
choices: 5′-ATGCCT-3′
3′-ATGCCT-5′
5′-TACGGA-3′
5′-AUGCCU-3′
items.explanation: Pairing T-A, A-T, C-G, G-C, G-C, A-T gives ATGCCT, and the new strand runs antiparallel to the template, so it is 5′-ATGCCT-3′. 3′-ATGCCT-5′ has the right bases but the wrong direction; U belongs in RNA.

items.prompt: Put these events of replication in order, for one stretch of new DNA on the lagging strand.
steps: Primase lays down a short RNA primer
DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the primer's 3′ end
The RNA primer is removed and replaced with DNA
DNA ligase seals the remaining nick
items.explanation: The strands must be separated before anything can pair with them. A primer gives polymerase a 3′ end, polymerase extends it, the primer is later swapped for DNA, and ligase makes the final bond.

items.prompt: After one round of replication of one DNA molecule, how many of the four strands in the two daughter molecules are newly made?
choices: One
Three
Two
Four
items.explanation: Each of the two daughter molecules has one old strand and one new one, so two of the four strands are new.

items.prompt: Which base is added to a new strand opposite a cytosine in the template?
items.explanation: Cytosine pairs with guanine, so polymerase adds a G opposite every C in the template.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: One DNA molecule is replicated twice. What fraction of all the strands is original parental DNA?
choices: None of the strands
items.explanation: Two rounds give 4 molecules, which is 8 strands. The two original strands are never broken up, so 2 of 8 strands, or 1/4, are parental.

items.prompt: Which isotope did Meselson and Stahl use to make the parent DNA heavy?
items.explanation: Bacteria grown on nitrogen-15 build it into their DNA bases, making the DNA denser than DNA made with ordinary nitrogen-14.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: After one generation in nitrogen-14, all the DNA formed a single band of intermediate density. Which model did this rule out?
choices: Semiconservative
Dispersive
Conservative
items.explanation: Conservative replication would keep one all-heavy molecule and make one all-light one, giving two bands. A single hybrid band fits both the semiconservative and dispersive models.

items.prompt: How did the second generation rule out the dispersive model?
choices: A heavy band appeared again, as if the parent DNA had been kept whole
Two bands appeared; dispersive predicts a single band
No DNA band appeared at all
Only a single heavy band appeared
items.explanation: Dispersive replication spreads old DNA through every molecule, so each generation would give one band that slowly gets lighter. Two separate bands, hybrid and light, fit only semiconservative replication.

items.prompt: If replication were conservative, what would Meselson and Stahl have seen after one generation?
choices: One band at hybrid density, between heavy and light
One light band
One heavy band
Two bands, one heavy and one light
items.explanation: Conservative replication keeps the parent helix whole, heavy, and builds an entirely new, light one, so there would be two bands. One hybrid band is what they actually saw.

items.prompt: Under semiconservative replication, what fraction of DNA molecules is hybrid after three generations in nitrogen-14?
items.explanation: After three generations there are 8 molecules. Only the 2 holding an original heavy strand are hybrid, so 2/8 = 1/4. The other 3/4 are light.

items.prompt: How did Meselson and Stahl separate DNA molecules of different density?
items.answer: By centrifuging them in a caesium chloride density gradient.
items.explanation: Spun at high speed, caesium chloride forms a gradient of density, and each DNA molecule settles where its density matches the solution's.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: Put the steps of the Meselson-Stahl experiment in order.
steps: Grow bacteria for many generations on nitrogen-15
Take samples after each round of division
Centrifuge the extracted DNA in a density gradient
items.explanation: First all the DNA had to be made heavy. Then the switch to light nitrogen meant all new DNA was light, and samples taken after each division were spun to measure their density.

items.prompt: How many origins of replication does the circular DNA of E. coli have?
choices: One
Two
Thousands
None; replication starts at random places
items.explanation: E. coli has a single origin, called oriC. Two forks leave it and meet on the far side of the circle. Thousands of origins is the eukaryotic pattern.

items.prompt: Why do eukaryotic cells start replication at many origins?
choices: Each origin copies one particular gene and no others
Their DNA polymerase can only copy a few hundred bases at a time
Their DNA is so long that one origin would take far too long
The origins hold the two strands together
items.explanation: Eukaryotic DNA is very long and its forks move fairly slowly, so copying from one origin would take weeks. Many origins working at once finish in hours. Origins are not tied to particular genes.

items.prompt: Origins of replication are often rich in A-T pairs. Why does this help?
choices: A-T pairs are where DNA ligase binds
A-T pairs have only two hydrogen bonds, so the strands separate easily
A-T pairs cannot be copied by polymerase, so the fork has to start there
A-T pairs are where the RNA primer is always laid
items.explanation: An A-T pair has two hydrogen bonds and a G-C pair three, so an A-T-rich stretch takes less energy to open, which is what an origin must do first.

items.prompt: When DNA opens at an origin, the separated strands form a loop with a fork at each end. What is it called?
items.explanation: The opened region is a replication bubble. It grows as its two forks move apart.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: From one origin of replication, how many forks move away, and in which directions?
items.answer: Two forks, moving away from the origin in opposite directions.
items.explanation: Replication is bidirectional: each bubble has a fork at each end, and both move outward from the origin.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: A bacterium's 4.6 million base pairs are copied from one origin by two forks, each moving at 1,000 base pairs per second. About how long does it take?
choices: About 77 minutes
About 38 minutes
About 19 minutes
About 5 seconds
items.explanation: The two forks share the work, so each copies 2.3 million base pairs: 2,300,000 ÷ 1,000 = 2,300 seconds, about 38 minutes. 77 minutes is the time for a single fork doing everything.

items.prompt: Put these events at an origin of replication in order.
steps: Initiator proteins bind to the origin sequence
The strands separate to open a small bubble
Helicases are loaded onto the separated strands
Two forks move away from the origin in opposite directions
items.explanation: Initiator proteins recognise the origin and pull the strands apart. Helicases are then loaded on the open DNA and drive the two forks outward.

verification.note: Set back to draft by the coordinator on 2026-11-10. Both solvers agreed with the key, but one pointed out the order is the bacterial one: in eukaryotes the helicase is loaded before the strands open. The prompt needs to say which.

items.prompt: What does helicase do at the replication fork?
choices: Separates the strands by breaking hydrogen bonds
Joins Okazaki fragments together into one strand
Lays down RNA primers
Adds nucleotides to the new strand
items.explanation: Helicase separates the strands by breaking the hydrogen bonds between bases. Ligase joins fragments, primase lays primers and DNA polymerase adds nucleotides.

items.prompt: Which bonds does helicase break to separate the two strands?
items.answer: The hydrogen bonds between paired bases.
items.explanation: Helicase breaks only the weak hydrogen bonds between bases. The covalent backbone of each strand stays intact.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: Tap DNA helicase.
items.explanation: Helicase is the ring at the point of the fork, where the parent helix is being split into two single strands.

items.prompt: Tap the single-strand binding proteins.
items.explanation: The small balls on the bare template strand are single-strand binding proteins. They keep it from pairing up again or folding back on itself.

items.prompt: Tap the enzyme that relieves twisting strain as the helix unwinds.
items.explanation: Topoisomerase sits on the unopened helix ahead of the fork. It cuts and rejoins DNA to relieve the overwinding that unzipping causes.

items.prompt: What would happen at the fork without single-strand binding proteins?
choices: Helicase could no longer use ATP to move along the DNA
Primers would be made too long
Ligase would join the fragments together in the wrong order
The strands would pair up again or fold on themselves
items.explanation: Single strands are sticky: their bases pair with whatever they can. The binding proteins coat them so they stay open for copying.

items.prompt: What supplies the energy helicase uses to separate the strands?
choices: Light absorbed by the DNA
Hydrolysis of ATP
Heat released by the cell
Breaking phosphodiester bonds in the backbone
items.explanation: Helicase splits ATP to drive itself along the DNA. It does not break the backbone; the phosphodiester bonds stay intact.

items.prompt: Unzipping overwinds the DNA ahead of the fork. Which enzyme relieves this by cutting and rejoining the DNA?
items.explanation: Topoisomerase breaks the backbone briefly, lets the strain unwind, then rejoins it. DNA gyrase is the bacterial topoisomerase that does this ahead of the fork.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: In which direction does DNA polymerase build a new strand?
choices: Either way, depending on the template
items.explanation: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to a 3′ end, so new strands always grow 5′ to 3′. The template is read 3′ to 5′, which is where the reverse answer comes from.

items.prompt: DNA polymerase adds each new nucleotide to which end of the growing strand?
items.explanation: It joins the new nucleotide's phosphate to the free 3′ hydroxyl of the last nucleotide in the strand.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: Tap the DNA polymerase building the leading strand.
items.explanation: DNA polymerase on the leading strand sits right behind the fork, adding nucleotides as the template is exposed.

items.prompt: What does DNA polymerase use as building blocks for new DNA?
choices: Amino acids
Ribonucleoside monophosphates such as AMP and GMP
Deoxynucleoside triphosphates such as dATP
Free bases without sugar or phosphate
items.explanation: Each building block is a deoxynucleoside triphosphate: a base, deoxyribose and three phosphates. Two phosphates are split off as it joins the strand.

items.prompt: When DNA polymerase adds a nucleotide, which molecule is released, supplying the energy for the new bond?
items.explanation: The incoming nucleotide is a triphosphate. Its outer two phosphates leave as pyrophosphate, and the energy released drives the new phosphodiester bond.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: DNA polymerase sometimes adds the wrong base. What does its proofreading do?
choices: Removes the wrong nucleotide and adds the right one
Cuts out the whole new strand and builds it again from the start
Leaves the mistake for ligase to fix
Changes the template base to match
items.explanation: Polymerase senses a mismatch, backs up and cuts the last nucleotide off the 3′ end, then tries again. Ligase only seals nicks; it does not check bases.

items.prompt: In which direction does DNA polymerase read its template strand?
items.explanation: The new strand grows 5′ to 3′ and is antiparallel to the template, so polymerase moves along the template from its 3′ end toward its 5′ end.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: Which enzyme makes RNA primers?
choices: Ligase
Helicase
Primase
Topoisomerase
items.explanation: Primase is an RNA polymerase that lays short primers on the template. Ligase seals gaps, helicase unwinds and topoisomerase relieves twisting.

items.prompt: Why does replication need a primer?
choices: DNA polymerase can only extend an existing 3′ end, not start a strand
The primer holds the two template strands apart
The primer marks which strand is the template
The primer protects the end of the new strand from being broken down by enzymes
items.explanation: DNA polymerase can add a nucleotide only to the 3′ hydroxyl of a strand already paired with the template. The primer provides that 3′ end. Holding the strands apart is the job of binding proteins.

items.prompt: Tap the RNA primer.
items.explanation: The primer is the short stretch at the start of the newest lagging-strand fragment. It is RNA, and DNA polymerase extends it with DNA.

items.prompt: How do the leading and lagging strands differ in how many primers they need?
choices: Both need one primer for every fragment
The leading strand needs no primer at all, because it is continuous
Both need exactly one primer
Leading: one at its start. Lagging: one per fragment
items.explanation: The leading strand is built in one piece, so it needs a single primer where it starts. Each Okazaki fragment on the lagging strand starts from its own primer.

items.prompt: In bacteria, which enzyme removes RNA primers and fills the gaps with DNA?
items.explanation: In bacteria DNA polymerase I removes the RNA nucleotides and replaces them with DNA. DNA polymerase III does the main copying.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: A primer is made of RNA. Which base can it contain that DNA does not?
choices: Thymine
Uracil
Guanine
Adenine
items.explanation: RNA uses uracil in place of thymine, so a primer pairs U with A in the template. Thymine is found in DNA, not RNA.

items.prompt: Order what happens to one primer and its fragment on the lagging strand.
steps: Primase builds the primer on the template
DNA polymerase extends the primer with DNA
The primer's RNA is removed and replaced with DNA
DNA ligase joins the fragment to its neighbour
items.explanation: The primer comes first, then DNA is added to its 3′ end. Once the next fragment reaches it, the RNA is swapped for DNA and ligase seals the last gap.

items.prompt: Why is the lagging strand made in short pieces?
choices: The lagging template is damaged and breaks into pieces
Polymerase builds only 5′ to 3′, which there points away from the fork
Helicase cuts the lagging strand as it unwinds
There is too little primase at the fork to make the lagging strand in one piece
items.explanation: On the lagging template, 5′ to 3′ synthesis heads away from the fork. As the fork opens more template, polymerase must start again near the fork, making one fragment at a time.

items.prompt: What are the short pieces of DNA made on the lagging strand called?
items.explanation: They are named after Reiji and Tsuneko Okazaki, who found them in the 1960s.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: Tap the finished Okazaki fragment.
items.explanation: The finished fragment is the stretch of new DNA between the polymerase and ligase on the lagging strand. Its primer has already been replaced.

items.prompt: Tap DNA ligase.
items.explanation: Ligase sits on the nick between two fragments of the lagging strand, where it makes the last backbone bond.

items.prompt: Tap the leading strand.
items.explanation: The leading strand is the long new strand built in one piece toward the fork, on the other arm from the fragments.

items.prompt: What does DNA ligase do?
choices: Removes RNA primers from the fragments
Unwinds the DNA ahead of the fork
Forms the hydrogen bonds between the new bases and the template strand
Seals the nick between fragments with a phosphodiester bond
items.explanation: Ligase closes the last gap in the backbone by making a phosphodiester bond. Primers are removed by a polymerase, and hydrogen bonds between bases form on their own.

items.prompt: Each Okazaki fragment grows in which direction relative to the moving fork?
choices: Away from the fork
Toward the fork
Both ways out from its primer
items.explanation: On the lagging template, 5′ to 3′ synthesis points away from the fork, so each fragment grows away from it. The leading strand is the one that grows toward the fork.

items.prompt: Which new strand is built continuously, toward the replication fork?
items.explanation: The leading strand's 5′ to 3′ direction points toward the fork, so polymerase can follow the fork without stopping.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

artifacts.title: The replication fork
artifacts.alt: A double helix on the left, with topoisomerase (a blue-grey diamond) on it, opens at helicase (a red ring) into two parent strands. Above, DNA polymerase (a sand oval) builds the long leading strand toward the fork. Below, small green binding proteins coat the bare template, then come a red RNA primer, a second polymerase, a finished Okazaki fragment, and DNA ligase (an ochre hexagon) on the gap to the next fragment.

artifacts.title: Copying DNA at the fork, step by step
artifacts.alt: Seven steps over the replication fork: topoisomerase relieves twisting, helicase unwinds the helix, binding proteins hold the strands apart, primase lays a primer, polymerase builds the leading strand, the lagging strand is made in Okazaki fragments, and ligase seals the gaps.

steps.title: Relieve the twisting
steps.text: Topoisomerase cuts and rejoins the DNA ahead of the fork, so the helix does not overwind as it is pulled open.

steps.title: Unwind
steps.text: Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs and separates the two parent strands.

steps.title: Hold the strands apart
steps.text: Single-strand binding proteins coat the bare strands so they do not pair up again.

steps.title: Lay a primer
steps.text: Primase builds a short RNA primer on the template, giving DNA polymerase a 3′ end to extend.

steps.title: Build the leading strand
steps.text: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides 5′ to 3′, building the leading strand in one piece toward the fork.

steps.title: Build the lagging strand
steps.text: On the other template polymerase works away from the fork, so it makes short Okazaki fragments.

steps.title: Seal the gaps
steps.text: Primers are replaced with DNA, and DNA ligase joins the fragments into one continuous strand.

artifacts.title: A replication bubble
artifacts.alt: A double helix drawn flat. In the middle the two dark green strands open into a bubble, with new blue-grey strands inside it. A red dot marks the origin at its centre, and arrows at each end show the two forks moving outward in opposite directions.

artifacts.title: Meselson and Stahl's results
artifacts.alt: Three centrifuge tubes for generations 0, 1 and 2 in nitrogen-14, with band positions marked light, hybrid and heavy. Generation 0 has one heavy band. Generation 1 has one hybrid band. Generation 2 has two bands, one hybrid and one light.
